intended_object: The determinant of an integral lattice (Ebeling, Lattices and Codes, Ch. 1): det of the Gram matrix (⟨e_i, e_j⟩) in any ℤ-basis of the lattice. It is an integer that does not depend on the basis. Inferred from the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
In this library, an `IntegralLattice V` is a full-rank ℤ-lattice (`Submodule.IsLattice ℚ`) in a ℚ-vector space, carrying a symmetric rational bilinear form that takes integer values on the lattice. Because the carrier is a lattice, it is a free, finitely generated ℤ-module, so `Module.Free.chooseBasis ℤ L` exists and has a finite index type.

The definition takes the determinant of the integral Gram matrix `L.integralForm (e i) (e j)` in that chosen basis. This is exactly the textbook determinant of a lattice. Using the chosen basis is harmless: the next result, `gramDet_eq_gramDet` / `determinant_eq_gramDet`, proves the value is the same in every basis, since a change of basis multiplies the determinant by (±1)² = 1.

Degenerate cases also come out right. For the zero lattice in the zero space, the Gram matrix is empty and its determinant is 1, which is the usual convention. For a degenerate form the determinant is 0, consistent with `determinant_ne_zero_iff`.

On generality: the definition depends on the library's own `IntegralLattice` structure. A rational ambient space is a standard setting for integral lattices. Mathlib has no lattice-determinant notion of this kind; `Algebra.discr` is about trace forms, which is a different object. So the definition is not too narrow.
